verses.text: Paul, called to be an apostle of Jesus Christ through the will of God, and our brother Sosthenes,
to the assembly of God which is at Corinth; those who are sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints, with all who call on the name of our Lord Jesus Christ in every place, both theirs and ours:
Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
I always thank my God concerning you, for the grace of God which was given you in Christ Jesus;
that in everything you were enriched in him, in all speech and all knowledge;
even as the testimony of Christ was confirmed in you:
so that you come behind in no gift; waiting for the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ;
who will also confirm you until the end, blameless in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.
God is faithful, through whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son, Jesus Christ, our Lord.

Now I beg you, brothers,  through the name of our Lord, Jesus Christ, that you all speak the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you, but that you be perfected together in the same mind and in the same judgment.
For it has been reported to me concerning you, my brothers, by those who are from Chloe’s household, that there are contentions among you.
Now I mean this, that each one of you says, “I follow Paul,” “I follow Apollos,” “I follow Cephas,” and, “I follow Christ.”
Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized into the name of Paul?
I thank God that I baptized none of you, except Crispus and Gaius,
so that no one should say that I had baptized you into my own name.
(I also baptized the household of Stephanas; besides them, I don’t know whether I baptized any other.)
For Christ sent me not to baptize, but to preach the Good News — not in wisdom of words, so that the cross of Christ wouldn’t be made void.
For the word of the cross is foolishness to those who are dying, but to us who are saved it is the power of God.
For it is written, “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, I will bring the discernment of the discerning to nothing.”
Where is the wise? Where is the scribe? Where is the lawyer of this world? Hasn’t God made foolish the wisdom of this world?
For seeing that in the wisdom of God, the world through its wisdom didn’t know God, it was God’s good pleasure through the foolishness of the preaching to save those who believe.
For Jews ask for signs, Greeks seek after wisdom,
but we preach Christ crucified; a stumbling block to Jews, and foolishness to Greeks,
but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God.
Because the foolishness of God is wiser than men, and the weakness of God is stronger than men.
For you see your calling, brothers, that not many are wise according to the flesh, not many mighty, and not many noble;
but God chose the foolish things of the world that he might put to shame those who are wise. God chose the weak things of the world, that he might put to shame the things that are strong;
and God chose the lowly things of the world, and the things that are despised, and the things that are not, that he might bring to nothing the things that are:
that no flesh should boast before God.
Because of him, you are in Christ Jesus, who was made to us wisdom from God, and righteousness and sanctification, and redemption:
that, according as it is written, “He who boasts, let him boast in the Lord.”

footnotes.content: Paul starts this letter by naming himself not by his past—'the Pharisee who killed Christians'—but by his calling. There's mercy in that. We too are known first by what Jesus has called us to, not by who we once were.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Corinth was a city of idols and trade-route excess. Yet Paul addresses those 'sanctified in Christ Jesus'—people who had turned from that world. What a word for them: you are already set apart, even as the pull of old habits still tugs.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Grace and peace—this greeting echoes the Old Testament shalom. Paul is saying: the ancient consolation of God still reaches you. Rest in that order: grace first (God's gift), peace second (your heart's settling).
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul always thanks God *before* correcting. Look at that humble order: gratitude precedes rebuke. When you must speak hard truth to someone, begin where Paul begins—with what you can honestly praise.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Corinthians were enriched in speech and knowledge—skilled debaters, clever teachers. But cleverness alone never fixed a broken church. That's the whole letter, really: gifts are good, but love is better.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The testimony of Christ was confirmed in them. What does that mean? That their lives bore witness—they lived differently because they'd met Jesus. No amount of smart talk replaces a changed heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They lacked no spiritual gift. Yet the church was fractured and confused. Sometimes the proudest gifts—prophecy, wisdom, tongues—can breed pride if they're not tethered to love and service.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jesus will confirm them until the end, blameless. What an anchor. Paul doesn't say they're blameless now; he says Christ's work will carry them through to the day of final reckoning. Hold fast to His faithfulness, not your own.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God is faithful—a real name for Him, proven across centuries. The fellowship of Jesus Christ isn't borrowed; it's grounded in God's own reliability. When your faith shakes, rest on His track record, not on your own steadiness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul begs them to be perfected together in the same mind. Not uniformity—diversity in a church is a gift—but unity of purpose. To follow Christ is to learn how to think and move as one body, despite different eyes and hands.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Chloe's household reported the divisions. A name, a real place, real people. Church problems aren't abstract—they involve mothers and servants, gossip and hurt feelings. Jesus still meets us in the messy details.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They split into factions: Paul's crowd, Apollos' admirers, Peter's followers, and the 'I follow Christ' group. Even claiming Jesus can become tribal. The moment we turn any teacher into our banner, we've missed the point.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Was Paul crucified for you? Did you take Paul's name in baptism? Three sharp questions that cut straight to the bone: only Christ died; only Christ was raised; only Christ claims your allegiance.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul names Crispus and Gaius by name—the few he baptized. He's not trying to take credit; he's showing restraint. When we do any good work, the more we can stay out of the spotlight, the clearer Christ becomes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He baptized almost nobody deliberately, so no one could say he'd baptized them into his own name. What humility—to build his own irrelevance into the work. That's the opposite of how we usually build kingdoms.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A parenthetical about Stephanas' household. The letter stays rooted in real stories, real families. God doesn't work in abstraction; He tends His flock member by member, household by household.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Christ sent him to preach, not to baptize—though baptism matters. The point: don't let ritual become substitute for the message. The cross itself is the real proclamation; ceremony serves it, never replaces it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: To those who are dying, the cross looks foolish. Of course—it offends human pride. But to those who are being saved, the same cross is God's power. It all hinges on whether you've surrendered your life to Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul quotes Isaiah: 'I will destroy the wisdom of the wise.' The prophets saw it coming—that God's ways overturn human cleverness. Pride in intellect is the oldest trap; God still unmakes it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Where are the wise, the scribes, the lawyers? Paul looks around a world full of bright minds—yet lost. No amount of reasoning solves what only grace can touch. The kingdom belongs to those willing to become fools for Christ.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The world's wisdom never found God. So God chose a different way: He reaches people through the 'foolishness' of preaching. A message, not an argument. Invitation, not proof. That's how grace works.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jews asked for signs; Greeks sought wisdom—two different hungers, both understandable, both missing the point. Paul names these ancient postures so we'll recognize them in ourselves.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A Messiah who died on a cross? Blasphemy to the Jew, absurdity to the Greek. But Paul preaches it anyway. Sometimes the truth sounds wrong to every part of us trained by the world's logic.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: To those called—Jews and Greeks both—Christ is power and wisdom. The same crucified Christ who offended them is their salvation. Calling changes everything. Once you're called, you see with new eyes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God's foolishness is wiser than human wisdom; God's weakness stronger than human strength. This isn't poetic exaggeration—it's literal. Our cleverest plans pale against His simplest move. Trust His apparent weakness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Not many of you were wise, mighty, or noble. The Corinthian church was mostly ordinary people—servants, traders, working folk. God doesn't call the elite to shame the elite; He calls the nobodies to show where real strength lies.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God chose the foolish and weak. Not because they're virtuous, but because they're the last place the world looks for power. When the gospel works through a nobody, nobody can claim it came from natural talent or breeding.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The lowly, the despised, the things that aren't—God chose them. He reaches for what the world discards. There's a strange tenderness there: the people you'd pass on the street, the ones with no name, those are the ones He calls His own.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: No flesh should boast before God. That's the aim of this whole reversal—to stop us in our pride. If salvation came through the clever and powerful, we'd have reason to strut. Instead, it comes to beggars, and beggars have nothing to brag about.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Because of Him, you are in Christ Jesus, who became wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, redemption. Jesus is not teaching those things; He *is* them. Your wholeness isn't a doctrine—it's a person, and His name is Jesus.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul quotes Jeremiah: 'He who boasts, let him boast in the Lord.' Our only legitimate pride is in God's faithfulness. When tempted to parade your gifts or achievements, remember—even your boasting should point away from you, to Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
